Mr. Vice President, distinguished delegates, colleagues, and friends. I begin by recommitting to defending the human rights of the people of Afghanistan, especially its women and girls, and by asking this Council to do the same, not only in words but also in deeds. We meet three weeks after the fifth anniversary of the Taliban's seizure of power. After five years, the cumulative effect is clear: the Taliban's unrelenting restrictions, policies, and practices not only violate the human rights of Afghans, but are reshaping the social fabric of the country. The education system excludes girls and indoctrinates boys. The media trumpets Taliban doctrine. Music, art, poetry, and other forms of culture are suppressed. The institutions that once offered protection have been dismantled, and now Taliban decrees reach into the most private areas of life. The Taliban are constantly testing the limits of what the international community will tolerate. After five years, they've learned that condemnation costs them little and that red lines can be crossed without consequences. Every time we protest in words but continue to act as before, we send the same message. This is acceptable. The Taliban's gender order is the center of it all. After four years in this mandate, I remain shocked by what Afghans share with me about physical and psychological abuse by Taliban officials, sometimes compounded by abuse from their own families. I'm also shocked by the increasingly dehumanizing statements of leading Taliban, including denying women's equal humanity. My report is in two parts. First, I review human rights developments since November 25, with an annex taking stock of the past five years. Second, I review the situation of children in Afghanistan. UN figures show that 46% of Afghans are under 15, two-thirds are under 25. Whatever happens to Afghanistan's children today will shape the country for decades to come. As with my previous reports, my findings come from Afghans themselves, focus group discussions with 102 participants from every region, and 25 written submissions, including from children and young people. The words of one girl have stayed with me. She said, "Three words have come to define our lives: fear, tears, and despair." Those are not simply the words of one girl. They reflect what I have been hearing from children and young people across Afghanistan about a childhood shaped by fear, deprivation, and loss of hope. I continue to hear reports of suicide by girls. The de facto authorities also continue to reject the internationally recognized definition of a child as anyone under 18, dismantling legal frameworks and institutions that used to protect children. At the same time, new directives and decrees are further eroding their rights. Their May 26 decree on spousal separation appears to recognize marriage involving children and treats any girl who's attained puberty as eligible. Under these rules, a girl's silence can be taken as her consent to marriage. It's become almost impossible for a married girl or woman to leave an abusive relationship. Meanwhile, the so-called rules for courts sanctions violence against women and girls with punishments only if there are broken bones or visible bruises. Even then, the penalties are grossly inadequate. While girls are excluded from secondary education, boys remain in school, but their education is increasingly shaped by Taliban ideology. My report finds that child labor is increasing despite being prohibited. Children sold or given away by families who've nothing left. Meanwhile, around 9 million Afghan children are facing severe hunger. and 3.7 million under five are acutely malnourished. My findings on children and youth include several intersecting identities and vulnerabilities. The harms to children can't be understood separately from gender, and the Taliban's institutionalized and systematic regime of gender-based discrimination, oppression, and domination which I've previously described as gender apartheid, is at the core of the Taliban's ideology and rule and is shaping the whole of society, including for children, with deeply intergenerational consequences. However, Afghans young people are not only victims. Girls are learning in secret and teaching one another. Young Afghans are documenting what's happening to them, organizing and finding ways to participate in their country's future. Behind this chamber, Afghan artists have an exhibition they cannot show at home. It's called Art Resists, Hope Blooms. I encourage you to see it. Now I'll briefly summarize some recent developments affecting the overall human rights situation. I'm deeply concerned about rising pressure on minority religious and ethnic communities. Afghans' right to practice their religion is being steadily constrained. A recent decree restricts recognition of preachers to followers of the Hanafi school, and the new family decree overrides Shia personal status law. In Barakshan, Ismaili places of worship continue to be closed. During Ashura this year, Shia commemorations were confined to designated locations, Mobile networks were suspended and dozens of men were detained for displaying Ashura flags. In April, 12 civilians were killed by unidentified gunmen near a Shia shrine in Hiraat. Minority communities are also targeted on ethnic grounds through land appropriation and forced evictions, exclusion from public life and other discriminatory practices. Pashtun and Hazara communities appear to be singled out, along with Uzbek, Turkmen and Tajik communities. I remain deeply concerned that persons who are or are perceived to be LGBTIQ+ remain extremely vulnerable to violence, discrimination and severe criminal punishment. Disability is a legacy of years of war. and people with disabilities are excluded from education, healthcare and assistance. I find children with disabilities face compounded barriers. Civic space has been steadily closed. Organizations, restricted journalists, detained human rights defenders, persecuted. When residents of Herat protested peacefully in June against the arrest of women of a dress requirement, security forces opened fire, killing a boy and detained dozens in the days that followed. And last month, the crackdown became law. A new statute approved by the Taliban leader bans all demonstrations throughout Afghanistan. And as I speak, six staff members of a humanitarian organization have been held for almost two months without charge. I call for their release and for the release of all civilians detained without trial. Cross-border attacks this year have killed or injured well over 1,000 civilians, many of them women and children, in their own homes. An air strike on a drug rehabilitation centre in Kabul on 16 March, according to UNAMA, killed 269 people and injured at least 122. I have not seen the outcome of an investigation into this tragedy. Millions of Afghans have come back from Iran and Pakistan, some deported, others under pressure. Among them are registered refugees, unaccompanied children and people born in exile. They arrived to find little work. and a humanitarian response a fraction of what is needed. Some returnees are punished for their past, links with the former republic, minorities or LGBTI identities, or lawful activity as defenders or journalists, punished through arbitrary detention, torture and, in some cases, death. I appreciate that Pakistan and Iran have hosted millions of Afghans for decades, and that Pakistan recently identified some 16,000 people whose stay is being facilitated. That instinct needs to become a system. No removal without individual protection screening. Afghanistan is not safe for involuntary return. Deportations must halt, including from European countries, which risk breaching the principle of non-refoulement. Mr. Vice President, I call on Member States to refrain from normalising relations with the Taliban until they have reversed oppressive policies. After five years, it may be tempting to think about a change in approach. However, neither dialogue with the Taliban nor isolating them appears to make any difference. There's no evidence that the Taliban intends to moderate its conduct. The decrees of the past year point in the other direction. There's a strong case for more humanitarian assistance and for well-designed support that reaches Afghans directly. But change must not mean compromising human rights law. Abandoning Afghans would hand the Taliban legitimacy in exchange for little, and Afghan women would pay first. And that standard applies to our own house. As the Secretary-General has noted, today is precisely one year since the Taliban physically barred Afghan women from reporting to the UN workplaces. We cannot keep asking States to refuse the erasure of women while accommodating it inside our own walls. The all-tools approach I espouse must advance gender-competent, survivor-centric, child-centred and inclusive justice, whoever the perpetrator and whenever the crime was committed. I call on Member States to urgently support and bolster every available accountability mechanism, and I hail Afghan-led efforts such as last year's hearing on the women of Afghanistan by the Permanent Peoples' Tribunal. In conclusion, five years is a long time in the life of a girl, but it is a short time in a country ravaged by decades of war and impunity. Victims and survivors of the entire period have a right to truth, justice and reparations. Once again, I ask this Council to stand with the people of Afghanistan in deeds as well as words. Thank you.
